claim: Up to 78% of patients with spinal cord injury develop spasticity within the first year.
source: Up to 78% of patients with spinal cord injury develop spasticity within the first year (Adams and Hicks, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adams and Hicks, 2005

claim: Spasticity is defined as a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes with exaggerated tendon jerks, resulting from hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex, and intermittent or sustained involuntary activation of muscles.
source: Spasticity is defined as a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes with exaggerated tendon jerks, resulting from hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex, and intermittent or sustained involuntary activation of muscles (Pandyan et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pandyan et al., 2005

claim: Current treatments like tizanidine, botulinum toxin and baclofen are only symptomatic, transiently effective and have varying side effects.
source: Current treatments like tizanidine, botulinum toxin and baclofen are only symptomatic, transiently effective and have varying side effects (Adams and Hicks, 2005; Thibaut et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adams and Hicks, 2005 and Thibaut et al., 2013

claim: Symptomatic treatments for spasticity rarely improve other functional disabilities associated with upper motor neuron lesions such as overground locomotion.
source: These symptomatic treatments, which aim at exaggerated reflexes and muscle tone, rarely improve other functional disabilities associated with upper motor neuron lesions such as overground locomotion (Dietz and Sinkjaer, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietz and Sinkjaer, 2007

claim: It remains challenging to model spastic behaviours in rodents.
source: However, it remains challenging to model spastic behaviours in rodents.
evidence: Statement of current state of the field based on established knowledge

claim: Upper arm spasticity after spinal cord injury and stroke often persists and hampers rehabilitation.
source: Upper arm spasticity after spinal cord injury and stroke often persists and hampers rehabilitation and effective new therapies are badly needed (Dietz and Fouad, 2014; Adams and Hicks, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dietz and Fouad, 2014 and Adams and Hicks, 2005

claim: Spastic behaviours examined in rat models include tail spasms and clonus.
source: To date, spastic behaviours that have been examined in rat models include tail spasms and clonus (Bennett et al., 2004, 1999) and spontaneous hindlimb and tail spasms during swimming (Gonzenbach et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett et al., 2004, 1999 and Gonzenbach et al., 2010

claim: Spastic behaviours examined in rat models include spontaneous hindlimb and tail spasms during swimming.
source: To date, spastic behaviours that have been examined in rat models include tail spasms and clonus (Bennett et al., 2004, 1999) and spontaneous hindlimb and tail spasms during swimming (Gonzenbach et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzenbach et al., 2010

claim: Sensory inputs from muscle spindles to the spinal cord play a major role in regulating spinal motor circuitry organization and output, especially after CNS injury.
source: Sensory inputs from muscles spindles to the spinal cord play a major role in regulating spinal motor circuitry organization and output, especially after CNS injury (Takeoka et al., 2014; Akay et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takeoka et al., 2014 and Akay et al., 2014

claim: Group I and II proprioceptive afferents innervating muscle spindles project via the dorsal root ganglia into the spinal cord to synapse onto motor neurons or interneurons.
source: Group I and II proprioceptive afferents innervating muscle spindles project via the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) into the spinal cord to synapse onto motor neurons or interneurons whilst Ib afferents from Golgi tendon organs form synapses on interneurons only (Eccles et al., 1957; Dietz, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eccles et al., 1957 and Dietz, 2002

claim: Ib afferents from Golgi tendon organs form synapses on interneurons only.
source: Group I and II proprioceptive afferents innervating muscle spindles project via the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) into the spinal cord to synapse onto motor neurons or interneurons whilst Ib afferents from Golgi tendon organs form synapses on interneurons only (Eccles et al., 1957; Dietz, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eccles et al., 1957 and Dietz, 2002

claim: Proprioceptive neurons provide positive feedback about muscle contractions, which adjusts movements to environmental factors and controls reflex responses via monosynaptic and polysynaptic spinal pathways.
source: Proprioceptive neurons provide positive feedback about muscle contractions, which adjusts movements to environmental factors and controls reflex responses via monosynaptic and polysynaptic spinal pathways (Dietz, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietz, 2002

claim: After traumatic brain or spinal cord injury, the circuits below the lesion site lose some supraspinal input, but they can reorganize and adapt.
source: After traumatic brain or spinal cord injury, the circuits below the lesion site lose some supraspinal input, but they can reorganize and adapt.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about neural plasticity after injury

claim: Proposed mechanisms of spasticity include increased activity and connectivity between proprioceptive Ia muscle afferents and motor neurons.
source: Proposed mechanisms of spasticity include increased activity and connectivity between proprioceptive Ia muscle afferents and motor neurons, reduced presynaptic inhibition of Ia afferents by spinal interneurons (Toda et al., 2014; Kakinohana et al., 2012), reduced autogenic inhibition from Golgi tendon organs (via Ib afferents and inhibitory interneurons), reduced reciprocal inhibition by Ia afferents from antagonist muscles and modified excitation and inhibition from muscle spindle group II afferents reviewed in [Nielsen et al., 2007; Dietz, 2002]) as well as intrinsic changes in motor neurons such as altered ion channels, serotonergic receptors and transporter concentrations in the membranes (Boulenguez et al., 2010; Murray et al., 2011) and an increase in persistent inward currents in motor neurons (Hultborn et al., 2013; Boulenguez et al., 2010; Bennett et al., 2001; ElBasiouny et al., 2010) which together cause an increase in motor neuron excitability.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Proposed mechanisms of spasticity include reduced presynaptic inhibition of Ia afferents by spinal interneurons.
source: Proposed mechanisms of spasticity include increased activity and connectivity between proprioceptive Ia muscle afferents and motor neurons, reduced presynaptic inhibition of Ia afferents by spinal interneurons (Toda et al., 2014; Kakinohana et al., 2012), reduced autogenic inhibition from Golgi tendon organs (via Ib afferents and inhibitory interneurons), reduced reciprocal inhibition by Ia afferents from antagonist muscles and modified excitation and inhibition from muscle spindle group II afferents reviewed in [Nielsen et al., 2007; Dietz, 2002]) as well as intrinsic changes in motor neurons such as altered ion channels, serotonergic receptors and transporter concentrations in the membranes (Boulenguez et al., 2010; Murray et al., 2011) and an increase in persistent inward currents in motor neurons (Hultborn et al., 2013; Boulenguez et al., 2010; Bennett et al., 2001; ElBasiouny et al., 2010) which together cause an increase in motor neuron excitability.
evidence: Supported by citations to Toda et al., 2014 and Kakinohana et al., 2012

claim: Proposed mechanisms of spasticity include an increase in persistent inward currents in motor neurons which cause an increase in motor neuron excitability.
source: Proposed mechanisms of spasticity include increased activity and connectivity between proprioceptive Ia muscle afferents and motor neurons, reduced presynaptic inhibition of Ia afferents by spinal interneurons (Toda et al., 2014; Kakinohana et al., 2012), reduced autogenic inhibition from Golgi tendon organs (via Ib afferents and inhibitory interneurons), reduced reciprocal inhibition by Ia afferents from antagonist muscles and modified excitation and inhibition from muscle spindle group II afferents reviewed in [Nielsen et al., 2007; Dietz, 2002]) as well as intrinsic changes in motor neurons such as altered ion channels, serotonergic receptors and transporter concentrations in the membranes (Boulenguez et al., 2010; Murray et al., 2011) and an increase in persistent inward currents in motor neurons (Hultborn et al., 2013; Boulenguez et al., 2010; Bennett et al., 2001; ElBasiouny et al., 2010) which together cause an increase in motor neuron excitability.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hultborn et al., 2013; Boulenguez et al., 2010; Bennett et al., 2001; ElBasiouny et al., 2010

claim: Peripherally derived Neurotrophin-3 is required for survival of large diameter sensory neurons and motor neurons.
source: Peripherally derived Neurotrophin-3, a nerve growth factor, is required for survival of large diameter sensory neurons and motor neurons (Ernfors et al., 1994; Woolley et al., 2005) and for correct patterning of central proprioceptive afferents during development (Patel et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ernfors et al., 1994 and Woolley et al., 2005

claim: Neurotrophin-3 is required for correct patterning of central proprioceptive afferents during development.
source: Peripherally derived Neurotrophin-3, a nerve growth factor, is required for survival of large diameter sensory neurons and motor neurons (Ernfors et al., 1994; Woolley et al., 2005) and for correct patterning of central proprioceptive afferents during development (Patel et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patel et al., 2003

claim: Neurotrophin-3 can reduce motor neuron excitability.
source: Neurotrophin-3 can also reduce motor neuron excitability (Petruska et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Petruska et al., 2010

claim: Neurotrophin-3 levels drop in the muscle after ensuring the survival and patterning of sensory and motor circuitry during development.
source: After ensuring the survival and patterning of sensory and motor circuitry during development, Neurotrophin-3 levels drop in the muscle (Murase et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murase et al., 1994

claim: Neurotrophin-3 levels are increased after exercise.
source: Interestingly, Neurotrophin-3 levels are again increased after exercise (Gómez-Pinilla et al., 2001; Ying et al., 2003), such as after rehabilitative training post-stroke or spinal cord injury (Hutchinson et al., 2004; Côté et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gómez-Pinilla et al., 2001 and Ying et al., 2003

claim: Neurotrophin-3 levels are increased after rehabilitative training post-stroke or spinal cord injury.
source: Interestingly, Neurotrophin-3 levels are again increased after exercise (Gómez-Pinilla et al., 2001; Ying et al., 2003), such as after rehabilitative training post-stroke or spinal cord injury (Hutchinson et al., 2004; Côté et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hutchinson et al., 2004 and Côté et al., 2011

claim: Rehabilitative training normalises proprioceptive reflexes in spinal cord injury models.
source: Rehabilitative training which is based on the principle that coordinated afferent input and motor output improves functional recovery (Frigon and Rossignol, 2006; Rossignol et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2006) also normalises proprioceptive reflexes in spinal cord injury models (Côté et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Côté et al., 2011

claim: Input from muscle afferents is important for maintaining normal locomotion in adult mice.
source: Input from muscle afferents is important for maintaining normal locomotion in adult mice (Akay et al., 2014) and for the reorganization of supraspinal pathways after spinal cord injury (because genetic deletion of muscle spindles leads to poorer outcomes [Takeoka et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Akay et al., 2014

claim: Genetic deletion of muscle spindles leads to poorer outcomes after spinal cord injury.
source: Input from muscle afferents is important for maintaining normal locomotion in adult mice (Akay et al., 2014) and for the reorganization of supraspinal pathways after spinal cord injury (because genetic deletion of muscle spindles leads to poorer outcomes [Takeoka et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takeoka et al., 2014

claim: Neurotrophin-3 is synthesized by muscle spindles in the periphery.
source: Neurotrophin-3 is synthesized by muscle spindles in the periphery (Copray and Brouwer, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Copray and Brouwer, 1994

claim: Peripherally administered Neurotrophin-3 can remodel spared corticospinal tract connections and promote sensorimotor recovery in adult and elderly rats after stroke.
source: Recent studies from our group show that peripherally administered Neurotrophin-3 can remodel spared corticospinal tract connections and promote sensorimotor recovery in adult and elderly rats after stroke (Duricki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duricki et al., 2016

claim: Peripheral treatment with recombinant Neurotrophin-3 has been tested in Phase I and II clinical trials and was found to be safe and well-tolerated.
source: Peripheral treatment with recombinant Neurotrophin-3 has already been tested in Phase I and II clinical trials and was found to be safe and well-tolerated (Parkman et al., 2003; Chaudhry et al., 2000; Coulie et al., 2000; Sahenk, 2007; Sahenk et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Parkman et al., 2003; Chaudhry et al., 2000; Coulie et al., 2000; Sahenk, 2007; Sahenk et al., 2005

claim: Neurotrophin-3 improved sensory and reflex function in patients with Charcot Marie Tooth 1A disease.
source: Interestingly, Neurotrophin-3 also improved sensory and reflex function in patients with Charcot Marie Tooth 1A disease, a large diameter fiber sensorimotor neuropathy (Sahenk et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sahenk et al., 2005

claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy in rats was sufficient to elicit changes in the connectivity of proprioceptive afferents to motor neurons resulting in signs of spasticity including hyperreflexia of mono- and polysynaptic reflexes.
source: Here, we established a novel rodent model of spasticity which displays many aspects of functional spasticity observed in humans. The model involves bilateral corticospinal tract lesioning in the pyramids, which was sufficient to elicit changes in the connectivity of proprioceptive afferents to motor neurons resulting in signs of spasticity including hyperreflexia of mono- and polysynaptic reflexes.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Intramuscular overexpression of Neurotrophin-3 normalized several spinal reflexes after bilateral pyramidotomy.
source: Intramuscular overexpression of Neurotrophin-3 normalized several spinal reflexes.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Neurotrophin-3 acts as a regulator of afferent input connectivity to spinal motor circuitry.
source: Analysis of neurophysiological properties of the spinal circuitry and of molecular markers revealed that Neurotrophin-3 acts as a regulator of afferent input connectivity to spinal motor circuitry and as a regulator of motor neuron excitability.
evidence: Based on experimental data and inference from results presented in the manuscript

claim: Neurotrophin-3 acts as a regulator of motor neuron excitability.
source: Analysis of neurophysiological properties of the spinal circuitry and of molecular markers revealed that Neurotrophin-3 acts as a regulator of afferent input connectivity to spinal motor circuitry and as a regulator of motor neuron excitability.
evidence: Based on experimental data and inference from results presented in the manuscript

claim: Bilateral transection of the pyramids confirmed that corticospinal tract fibers running ventrally through the pyramids had been cut.
source: The lesion completeness was assessed for all rats at the end of the study with eriochrome cyanine staining of the medulla, which confirmed that corticospinal tract fibers running ventrally through the pyramids had been cut (Figure 1B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on histological data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The left and right pyramids were almost completely absent in bPYX GFP rats versus uninjured naïve rats.
source: (C) The left and right pyramids were almost completely absent in bPYX GFP rats versus uninjured naïve rats (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 107.4, p<0.0001; bPYX GFP versus naïve p<0.001).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of histological data shown in Figure 1C

claim: A greater percentage of bPYX GFP rats exhibited flexor spasms than the percentage that exhibited extensor spasms two weeks post-injury.
source: (D) A greater percentage of bPYX GFP rats exhibited flexor spasms than the percentage that exhibited extensor spasms two weeks post-injury.
evidence: Based on behavioral observation data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Rats showed abnormal forelimb movements and signs of spasticity in the open field after bPYX.
source: (E) Rats showed abnormal forelimb movements and signs of spasticity in the open field after bPYX (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 19.8, p<0.001; bPYX GFP baseline versus all post-injury Weeks, paired t-test p-values<0.05).
evidence: Based on behavioral scoring data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy caused rats to make many errors on the horizontal ladder with their treated forelimb as a percentage of the total steps taken.
source: (F) Bilateral pyramidotomy caused rats to make many errors on the horizontal ladder with their treated forelimb as a percentage of the total steps taken (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 123.4, p<0.001; bPYX GFP vs naïve p<0.0001; bPYX GFP vs naïve at Weeks 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, p-values<0.05).
evidence: Based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 1F

claim: bPYX rats had reduced grip strength with their treated forepaw at Weeks 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 versus uninjured naïves.
source: (G) Unilateral Grip Strength Test. bPYX rats had reduced grip strength with their treated forepaw at Weeks 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 versus uninjured naïves (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 145.0, p<0.001; bPYX GFP vs naïve p<0.0001; bPYX GFP vs naïve at Weeks 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, p-values<0.05).
evidence: Based on grip strength testing data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy caused slight mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: (H) Responses to mechanical stimulation of the treated forepaw were assessed using the automated von Frey test. Bilateral pyramidotomy caused slight mechanical hypersensitivity (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 5.2, p=0.019; bPYX GFP vs naïve p = 0.003; bPYX GFP versus naïve at Week 4 and 8, p-values<0.05)
evidence: Based on von Frey testing data shown in Figure 1H

claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy led to a persistent deficit in dexterity.
source: (I) Montoya Staircase Pellet Reaching Test. This test assesses fine motor function of the distal forelimb. The sucrose pellets that were eaten on the treated side were counted. Bilateral pyramidotomy led to a persistent deficit in dexterity (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 100.3, p<0.0001; bPYX GFP vs naïve p<0.0001; bPYX GFP versus naïve at weeks 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 post-injury p-values<0.0001).
evidence: Based on staircase pellet reaching test data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Less H-wave depression was observed in bPYX GFP rats two weeks post injury compared to uninjured naïve rats.
source: (K) Frequency-dependent depression: The H-wave was depressed at short inter-stimulus intervals in uninjured naïve rats. Less H-wave depression was observed in bPYX GFP rats two weeks post injury (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 9.8, p<0.0001; uninjured versus bPYX GFP at 2 s, 1 s, 0.5 s, 0.2 s and 0.1 s inter-stimulus interval p-values<0.05).
evidence: Based on H-reflex electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1K

claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy caused an increase in hyperreflexia relative to uninjured naïve rats at week 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.
source: (L) Data for each rat at each week was analysed by measuring the area under each curve which gives an electrophysiological correlate of hyperreflexia. Bilateral pyramidotomy caused an increase in hyperreflexia relative to uninjured naïve rats at week 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 5.9, p<0.001; bPYX GFP versus naïve p = 0.003; bPYX GFP versus naïve at weeks 2, 6 and 10 post-injury, p-values<0.05).
evidence: Based on H-reflex area under curve analysis shown in Figure 1L

claim: bPYX GFP rats had an increased polysynaptic reflex response when the median nerve was stimulated and responses were recorded from the ulnar nerve.
source: (Q) The polysynaptic compound action potentials were quantified by measuring the absolute integral (area under the rectified curve) from 3.5 ms to 12 ms. bPYX GFP rats had an increased polysynaptic reflex response (one-way ANOVA F-value = 4.8, p=0.02; bPYX GFP versus naïve, p-value = 0.02).
evidence: Based on nerve stimulation electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1Q

claim: bPYX GFP rats had increased polysynaptic responses when the radial nerve was stimulated and responses were recorded from the ulnar nerve.
source: (U) The polysynaptic compound action potentials were quantified by measuring the absolute integral (area under the rectified curve) from 3.5 ms to 12 ms. bPYX GFP rats had increased polysynaptic responses versus uninjured naïve rats (one-way ANOVA F-value = 4.2, p=0.03; bPYX GFP versus naïve, p-value = 0.01).
evidence: Based on nerve stimulation electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1U

claim: Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in treated muscles at 10 weeks after AAV1-NT3 injection.
source: At the end of the study, Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assays (ELISAs) showed that Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in treated muscles (e.g., in the ipsilateral but not contralateral biceps brachii) (Figure 2B) as well as in the blood (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in the blood at 10 weeks after AAV1-NT3 injection.
source: At the end of the study, Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assays (ELISAs) showed that Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in treated muscles (e.g., in the ipsilateral but not contralateral biceps brachii) (Figure 2B) as well as in the blood (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in ipsilateral cervical C3-C8 DRGs at 4 weeks after AAV1-NT3 injection.
source: ELISA showed that Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in ipsilateral (but not contralateral) cervical C3-C8 DRGs (Figure 2D), consistent with retrograde transport of hypothetically either AAV1 particles and/or Neurotrophin-3 protein itself.
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The AAV1 vector carrying the transgene was not retrogradely transported to the DRG.
source: We found that the AAV1 vector carrying the transgene was not retrogradely transported to the DRG (Figure 2E).
evidence: Based on qRTPCR data shown in Figure 2E showing absence of human NT-3 mRNA in DRGs

claim: Human Neurotrophin-3 mRNA was not detected in the ipsilateral or contralateral cervical DRGs of rats injected with AAV1-NT3 or AAV1-GFP.
source: In other words, we did not detect human Neurotrophin-3 mRNA in the ipsilateral or contralateral cervical DRGs of rats injected with AAV1-NT3 or AAV1-GFP (Figure 2E) although we did detect a strong signal for human Neurotrophin-3 in positive control samples of human brain cDNA.
evidence: Based on qRTPCR data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The viral vector itself was not retrogradely transported to the DRG, but the neurotrophin-3 protein itself was.
source: Together these results show that the viral vector itself was not retrogradely transported to the DRG, but the neurotrophin-3 protein itself was.
evidence: Based on inference from qRTPCR and ELISA data

claim: Intramuscular treatment using AAV1-NT3 did not significantly increase levels of Neurotrophin-3 protein in homogenates of ipsilateral or contralateral spinal cervical hemicords 4 weeks after injection.
source: Intramuscular treatment using AAV1-NT3 in this cohort did not significantly increase levels of Neurotrophin-3 protein in homogenates of ipsilateral or contralateral spinal cervical hemicords (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) or liver (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) 4 weeks after injection.
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: In rats treated with AAV1-NT3, Neurotrophin-3 protein was increased in neurons of the ipsilateral cervical dorsal horn.
source: Immunolabeling revealed that, in rats treated with AAV1-NT3, Neurotrophin-3 protein was increased in neurons of the ipsilateral cervical dorsal horn (Figure 2H) and ipsilateral cervical motor neurons (including in their nuclei) (Figure 2J) relative to AAV1-GFP (Figure 2G,I respectively) but not in contralateral dorsal horn or motor neurons.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2H

claim: In rats treated with AAV1-NT3, Neurotrophin-3 protein was increased in ipsilateral cervical motor neurons.
source: Immunolabeling revealed that, in rats treated with AAV1-NT3, Neurotrophin-3 protein was increased in neurons of the ipsilateral cervical dorsal horn (Figure 2H) and ipsilateral cervical motor neurons (including in their nuclei) (Figure 2J) relative to AAV1-GFP (Figure 2G,I respectively) but not in contralateral dorsal horn or motor neurons.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2J

claim: Neurotrophin-3 treatment led to a reduction of forelimb spasticity which was still ongoing at 10 weeks post-injury and treatment.
source: Neurotrophin-3 treatment led to a reduction of forelimb spasticity which was still ongoing at 10 weeks post-injury and treatment (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on behavioral scoring data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Neurotrophin-3 treatment reduced signs of spasticity.
source: (A) Neurotrophin-3 treatment reduced signs of spasticity (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 19.8, p<0.001; bPYX NT3 versus bPYX GFP at Week 6, 8 and 10, p-values<0.05).
evidence: Based on behavioral scoring data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 treatment gradually improved precision stepping on the horizontal ladder throughout the 10 weeks testing period.
source: Rats with bilateral pyramidotomy treated with AAV-GFP frequently missed rungs, but intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 treatment gradually improved precision stepping on the horizontal ladder throughout the 10 weeks testing period (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on horizontal ladder test data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Neurotrophin-3 treated rats partially recovered grip strength with their treated forelimb.
source: Additionally, Neurotrophin-3 treated rats partially recovered grip strength with their treated forelimb (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on grip strength test data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Neurotrophin-3 did not cause or affect mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: Importantly, Neurotrophin-3 did not cause or affect mechanical hypersensitivity, as expected from human clinical trials (Parkman et al., 2003; Sahenk, 2007; Chaudhry et al., 2000; Coulie et al., 2000; Sahenk et al., 2005) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on von Frey test data shown in Figure 3D and supported by citations to clinical trials

claim: Intramuscular AAV-NT3 treatment did not improve recovery on the pellet reaching task after bilateral pyramidotomy.
source: Intramuscular AAV-NT3 treatment did not improve recovery on the pellet reaching task after bilateral pyramidotomy (Figure 3E) which is consistent with the fact that corticospinal injury leads to a persistent deficit in dexterity (Weidner et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on staircase pellet reaching test data shown in Figure 3E and supported by citation to Weidner et al., 2001

claim: Intramuscular overexpression of Neurotrophin-3 restored the frequency-dependent depression of the H-wave by 6 weeks post-injury.
source: As described above, rats showed less H-wave depression at inter-stimulus intervals of 5 s and less after bilateral pyramidotomy. Intramuscular overexpression of Neurotrophin-3 restored the frequency-dependent depression of the H-wave by 6 weeks post-injury (Figure 3F,G, Table 1), consistent with injection of AAV-NT3 into this hand muscle.
evidence: Based on H-reflex electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3G and Table 1

claim: Neurotrophin-3 normalised the exaggerated polysynaptic responses that were measured in the ulnar nerve after median nerve stimulation.
source: Neurotrophin-3 treatment also modified polysynaptic spinal reflexes involving afferents from treated muscles. Neurotrophin-3 normalised the exaggerated polysynaptic responses that were measured in the ulnar nerve after median nerve stimulation (Figure 3I–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on nerve stimulation electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3J

claim: Neurotrophin-3 treated animals had no reduction of the exaggerated polysynaptic responses recorded in the ulnar nerve after radial nerve stimulation.
source: However, Neurotrophin-3 treated animals had no reduction of the exaggerated polysynaptic responses recorded in the ulnar nerve after radial nerve stimulation (Figure 3K–L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the fact that only flexor muscles were injected with AAV-NT3 and that proprioceptive afferent fibers in the radial nerve (supplying extensor muscles) did not receive direct treatment.
evidence: Based on nerve stimulation electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3L and inference about treatment specificity

claim: After bilateral pyramidotomy, more vGluT1 boutons were found in close proximity to cervical motor neurons of the ulnar and radial nerves.
source: We determined whether the number of vGluT1 immunoreactive boutons in close proximity to motor neurons changed after bilateral pyramidotomy (Figure 4A–C). After injury, more vGluT1 boutons were found in close proximity to cervical motor neurons of the ulnar and radial nerves (Figure 4E) which might contribute to the spasticity we report.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4E

claim: CTb-immunoreactive afferents from the ulnar nerve had more vGluT1 boutons in close proximity to radial motor neurons after bilateral pyramidotomy.
source: CTb-immunoreactive afferents from the ulnar nerve had more vGluT1 boutons in close proximity to radial motor neurons (Figure 4F). This suggests aberrant strengthening of excitatory afferent connectivity upon antagonists which might mediate increased co-contractions.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4F and inference about functional consequences

claim: After bilateral pyramidotomy, there were fewer vGAT boutons in close proximity to vGluT1 positive boutons.
source: Analysis of z-stack confocal images revealed vGAT immunoreactive boutons in close proximity to vGluT1 immunoreactive boutons in the ventral horn. After bilateral pyramidotomy, there were fewer vGAT boutons in close proximity to vGluT1 positive boutons (Figure 4K) suggesting they received less presynaptic inhibition by GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4K and inference about presynaptic inhibition

claim: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 normalized the number of excitatory vGluT1 boutons onto ulnar and radial motor neurons.
source: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 normalized the number of excitatory vGluT1 boutons onto ulnar and radial motor neurons (Figure 4D–E), reduced CTb+ ulnar excitatory boutons near to radial motor neurons towards the levels seen in uninjured naïve rats (Figure 4F) and increased apparent presynaptic inhibition of vGluT1 boutons to normal levels (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4E

claim: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 reduced CTb+ ulnar excitatory boutons near to radial motor neurons towards the levels seen in uninjured naïve rats.
source: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 normalized the number of excitatory vGluT1 boutons onto ulnar and radial motor neurons (Figure 4D–E), reduced CTb+ ulnar excitatory boutons near to radial motor neurons towards the levels seen in uninjured naïve rats (Figure 4F) and increased apparent presynaptic inhibition of vGluT1 boutons to normal levels (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4F

claim: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 increased apparent presynaptic inhibition of vGluT1 boutons to normal levels.
source: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 normalized the number of excitatory vGluT1 boutons onto ulnar and radial motor neurons (Figure 4D–E), reduced CTb+ ulnar excitatory boutons near to radial motor neurons towards the levels seen in uninjured naïve rats (Figure 4F) and increased apparent presynaptic inhibition of vGluT1 boutons to normal levels (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4K

claim: The number of vGAT immunoreactive inhibitory boutons upon motor neurons was not affected by injury or Neurotrophin-3 treatment.
source: The number of vGAT immunoreactive inhibitory boutons upon motor neurons which mediate post-synaptic inhibition was not affected by injury or Neurotrophin-3 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Corticospinal tract injury resulted in an increase of serotonergic fiber density in the ventral horn, but not in the dorsal horn.
source: Cervical spinal cord sections were immunolabeled for serotonin and we measured the pixel intensity in the dorsal laminae I/II/III and the ventral horn. Corticospinal tract injury resulted in an increase of serotonergic fiber density in the ventral horn, but not in the dorsal horn; the former was normalized by Neurotrophin-3 treatment (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 5B

claim: Neurotrophin-3 treatment normalized the increase of serotonergic fiber density in the ventral horn.
source: Cervical spinal cord sections were immunolabeled for serotonin and we measured the pixel intensity in the dorsal laminae I/II/III and the ventral horn. Corticospinal tract injury resulted in an increase of serotonergic fiber density in the ventral horn, but not in the dorsal horn; the former was normalized by Neurotrophin-3 treatment (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 5B

claim: After injury, there was less KCC2 in the membrane of ulnar and radial motor neurons and more accumulations within the somata.
source: After injury, we found less KCC2 in the membrane of ulnar and radial motor neurons and more accumulations within the somata (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 5C,D

claim: Neurotrophin-3 treatment translocated KCC2 back to the membrane of both ulnar and radial motor neurons.
source: Neurotrophin-3 treatment translocated KCC2 back to the membrane of both ulnar and radial motor neurons (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: Selective and complete lesioning of the corticospinal tract results in spasticity in the rodent model.
source: Our rodent model gives evidence that selective and complete lesioning of the corticospinal tract results in spasticity.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: Damage to the pyramidal tracts is sufficient and necessary to cause spastic hemiplegia in humans.
source: Spasticity symptoms have sometimes been ascribed to additional damage to extrapyramidal structures, but a recent extensive review of pathological cases gives evidence that damage to the pyramidal tracts is sufficient and necessary to cause spastic hemiplegia in humans (de Oliveira-Souza, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Oliveira-Souza, 2015

claim: Macaque monkeys with bilateral corticospinal tract injuries in the pyramids were still able to walk and climb shortly after the injury.
source: A large cohort of macaque monkeys received bilateral corticospinal tract injuries in the pyramids. While skilled hand function is severely affected by the lesions, the monkeys were still able to walk and climb shortly after the injury.
evidence: Based on reference to Lawrence and Kuypers' classic experiments

claim: Macaque monkeys with bilateral pyramidotomy exhibited clonic movements, narrowed stance during locomotion, and increased flexor activities in their forelimbs.
source: We re-examined their original videos (Lemon et al., 2012) and observed clonic movements (their Supplementary Videos 2, 3 and 8), narrowed stance during locomotion (their Supplementary Video 6) and increased flexor activities in their forelimbs (their Supplementary Video 7) supporting the notion that corticospinal tract injury is sufficient to produce spastic signs and abnormal locomotion in non-human primates as well as humans.
evidence: Based on re-examination of videos from Lemon et al., 2012

claim: After thoracic cord transection or contusion, rats show lower limb spasticity.
source: After thoracic cord transection or contusion, rats show lower limb spasticity (Côté et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 1998; Bose et al., 2002; Corleto et al., 2015; Yates et al., 2008) and after sacral cord transection rodents displayed tail spasms (Bennett et al., 2004; Kapitza et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: After sacral cord transection rodents displayed tail spasms.
source: After thoracic cord transection or contusion, rats show lower limb spasticity (Côté et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 1998; Bose et al., 2002; Corleto et al., 2015; Yates et al., 2008) and after sacral cord transection rodents displayed tail spasms (Bennett et al., 2004; Kapitza et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett et al., 2004; Kapitza et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2010

claim: A midthoracic T-lesion results in hindlimb spasms during swimming.
source: A midthoracic T-lesion, which essentially damages the dorsomedial, dorsolateral and ventromedial parts of the corticospinal tracts, results in hindlimb spasms during swimming (Gonzenbach et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzenbach et al., 2010

claim: Baclofen is one of the more potent anti-spasticity drugs.
source: One of the more potent anti-spasticity drugs is baclofen, a GABAB receptor agonist (Stempien and Tsai, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stempien and Tsai, 2000

claim: Spasticity is associated with a decrease of inhibitory synapses and inhibitory post-synaptic potentials in motor neurons.
source: Spasticity is associated with a decrease of inhibitory synapses and inhibitory post-synaptic potentials in motor neurons (Kapitza et al., 2012; Kakinohana et al., 2012; Boulenguez et al., 2010) plus concurrent increase of excitatory synapses upon and persistent inward currents in motor neurons (Tan et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2001; Hultborn et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kapitza et al., 2012; Kakinohana et al., 2012; Boulenguez et al., 2010

claim: Spasticity is associated with an increase of excitatory synapses upon and persistent inward currents in motor neurons.
source: Spasticity is associated with a decrease of inhibitory synapses and inhibitory post-synaptic potentials in motor neurons (Kapitza et al., 2012; Kakinohana et al., 2012; Boulenguez et al., 2010) plus concurrent increase of excitatory synapses upon and persistent inward currents in motor neurons (Tan et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2001; Hultborn et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tan et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2001; Hultborn et al., 2013

claim: Knocking out presynaptic GABAergic interneurons results in limb oscillations during directed reaching for sugar pellets.
source: Functionally, knocking out presynaptic GABAergic interneurons results in limb oscillations during directed reaching for sugar pellets (Fink et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fink et al., 2014

claim: Mice lacking functional muscle spindles show impaired re-organization of spinal circuitry and restricted locomotor recovery after CNS injury.
source: Indeed, mice lacking functional muscle spindles (lacking proprioceptive feedback) show impaired re-organization of spinal circuitry and restricted locomotor recovery after CNS injury (Takeoka et al., 2014; Akay et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takeoka et al., 2014 and Akay et al., 2014

claim: Corticospinal axons and proprioceptive afferents compete for synaptic space in the spinal cord in development and also in adulthood.
source: Corticospinal axons and proprioceptive afferents compete for synaptic space in the spinal cord in development and also in adulthood (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2016

claim: Premotor interneurons receive direct input from the corticospinal tract and cutaneous and proprioceptive afferent fibers.
source: Premotor interneurons receive direct input from the corticospinal tract and cutaneous and proprioceptive afferent fibers (Brownstone and Bui, 2010); following loss of corticospinal input, proprioceptive afferents may invade the empty synaptic space on these interneurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brownstone and Bui, 2010 and inference about consequences of injury

claim: Following loss of corticospinal input, proprioceptive afferents may invade the empty synaptic space on premotor interneurons.
source: Premotor interneurons receive direct input from the corticospinal tract and cutaneous and proprioceptive afferent fibers (Brownstone and Bui, 2010); following loss of corticospinal input, proprioceptive afferents may invade the empty synaptic space on these interneurons.
evidence: Inference based on known anatomy and competition for synaptic space

claim: Motor neurons, low threshold cutaneous mechanoceptive afferents and proprioceptive afferents express trkC.
source: Motor neurons, low threshold cutaneous mechanoceptive afferents and proprioceptive afferents express trkC (McMahon et al., 1994), which is the main receptor for neurotrophin-3.
evidence: Supported by citation to McMahon et al., 1994

claim: Neurotrophins are retrogradely transported in signaling endosomes after they bind to and are internalized with their receptors.
source: Neurotrophins are retrogradely transported in signaling endosomes (after they bind to and are internalized with their receptors) (Helgren et al., 1997; Harrington et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Helgren et al., 1997; Harrington et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2010

claim: Cutaneous afferents may have modulated spinal reflexes after NT-3 treatment.
source: We expect that the majority of changes in spinal cord patterning and excitability was mediated via proprioceptive afferents and motor neurons. However, we cannot exclude the possibilities that cutaneous afferents may have modulated spinal reflexes (Bui et al., 2013) as it is likely that skin afferents were also exposed to a low concentration of Neurotrophin-3; or that neurotrophin-3 acted to some degree through the vascular circulation systemically although we didn't detect a significant increase protein in muscles other than the injected ones or in the spinal cord.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms, supported by citation to Bui et al., 2013

claim: Neurotrophin-3 had several effects on spinal networks that likely contributed to normalization of mono- and polysynaptic reflexes and resulted in functional recovery.
source: Neurotrophin-3 had several effects on spinal networks that likely contributed to normalization of mono- and polysynaptic reflexes and resulted in functional recovery.
evidence: Summary inference based on multiple experimental findings in the study

claim: Neurotrophin-3 caused a re-balancing of excitatory and inhibitory networks in the spinal cord.
source: Firstly, Neurotrophin-3 caused a re-balancing of excitatory and inhibitory networks in the spinal cord. It restored the specificity and number of excitatory boutons from proprioceptive axons onto motor neurons and a marker of presynaptic inhibition to normal.
evidence: Based on experimental data from immunohistochemistry studies

claim: Neurotrophin-3 normalised the levels of KCC2 in ulnar and radial motor neuron membranes to normal.
source: Secondly, neurotrophin-3 normalised the levels of KCC2 in ulnar and radial motor neuron membranes to normal.
evidence: Based on experimental data from immunohistochemistry studies

claim: Neurotrophin-3 normalized the pattern of serotonergic fibers in the cervical spinal cord.
source: Finally, neurotrophin-3 also affected plasticity of extrapyramidal supraspinal pathways. We showed that neurotrophin-3 normalized the pattern of serotonergic fibers in the cervical spinal cord.
evidence: Based on experimental data from immunohistochemistry studies

claim: Rubrospinal tract neurons express trkC receptors.
source: Given that other pathways like rubrospinal tract neurons also express trkC receptors (Tetzlaff et al., 1994; King et al., 1999) it is possible that these pathways also undergo sprouting within the cervical spinal cord and may contribute to functional recovery (Raineteau et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tetzlaff et al., 1994 and King et al., 1999

claim: Neurorehabilitative training ameliorates reflexes.
source: This improves locomotor function. Motor function and restoration of normal reflexes are interdependent and mutually reinforcing as it has been shown that neurorehabilitative training ameliorates reflexes (Côté et al., 2011) and reflex training ameliorates neurorehabilitation (Thompson and Wolpaw, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Côté et al., 2011

claim: Reflex training ameliorates neurorehabilitation.
source: This improves locomotor function. Motor function and restoration of normal reflexes are interdependent and mutually reinforcing as it has been shown that neurorehabilitative training ameliorates reflexes (Côté et al., 2011) and reflex training ameliorates neurorehabilitation (Thompson and Wolpaw, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thompson and Wolpaw, 2015

claim: Existing anti-spastic treatments often do not improve the movement disorder.
source: Existing anti-spastic treatments, which reduce exaggerated reflexes and muscle tone, often do not improve the movement disorder (Dietz and Sinkjaer, 2007; Corry et al., 1997; Latash and Penn, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dietz and Sinkjaer, 2007; Corry et al., 1997; Latash and Penn, 1996

claim: Intramuscular neurotrophin-3 not only normalized reflexes, but also improved locomotion and grip strength.
source: Here, we have shown intramuscular treatment with neurotrophin-3 not only normalized reflexes, but also improved locomotion and grip strength.
evidence: Based on experimental data from behavioral tests in the study

claim: Intramuscular neurotrophin-3 improved fine motor function and tactile sensation in adult and elderly rats after stroke.
source: In previous studies, our group used delayed, intramuscular neurotrophin-3 to treat stroke and observed improved fine motor function and tactile sensation in adult and elderly rats (Duricki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duricki et al., 2016

claim: A gene therapy involving intramuscular injection of an AAV1 encoding human neurotrophin-3 has FDA approval for a clinical trial for patients with Charcot Marie Tooth 1A.
source: Moreover, a gene therapy involving intramuscular injection of an AAV1 encoding human neurotrophin-3 under the control of a muscle-specific promoter, which was successfully tested in a mouse model of Charcot Marie Tooth neuropathy (Sahenk et al., 2014), now has FDA approval for a clinical trial for patients with Charcot Marie Tooth 1A (Professor Zarife Sahenk, personal communication, August 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sahenk et al., 2014 and personal communication

claim: 60 female Lister hooded rats were used in the study.
source: 60 female Lister hooded rats (Charles River; outbred; 190–250 g) were used.
evidence: Statement of experimental methods

claim: The group size was 10 or more rats per treatment.
source: Generally, the group size was 10 or more rats per treatment in line with previous spinal cord injury/ stroke in vivo studies (Duricki et al., 2016; Kathe et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement of experimental design, supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Three days prior to terminal electrophysiology experiments, ulnar and radial motor neurons were retrogradely traced.
source: Three days prior to terminal electrophysiology experiments, we retrogradely traced ulnar (flexor) and radial (extensor) motor neurons.
evidence: Statement of experimental methods

claim: The H-reflex was assessed at baseline and every two weeks post-surgery.
source: The H-reflex was assessed at baseline and every two weeks post-surgery.
evidence: Statement of experimental methods

claim: vGluT1 is located in excitatory boutons of proprioceptive and cutaneous mechanosensory axons.
source: Transverse sections of the cervical spinal cord were immunolabeled for vGluT1 which is located in excitatory boutons of proprioceptive and cutaneous mechanosensory axons (Alvarez et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alvarez et al., 2011

claim: In the intact rat, vGluT1 boutons on motor neurons are from proprioceptive afferents.
source: In the intact rat, vGluT1 boutons on motor neurons are from proprioceptive afferents (Stepien et al., 2010; Betley et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stepien et al., 2010 and Betley et al., 2009

claim: Synapses from primary afferents onto motor neurons are often modulated by inhibitory synapses from GABAergic interneurons onto the afferent axon terminals.
source: Synapses from primary afferents onto motor neurons (i.e., proprioceptive afferents) are often modulated by inhibitory synapses from GABAergic interneurons onto the afferent axon terminals (Figure 4G) (Fink et al., 2014; Betley et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fink et al., 2014 and Betley et al., 2009

claim: Complete transection causes an up-regulation of the constitutively active 5HT2C receptor.
source: Complete transection causes an up-regulation of the constitutively active 5HT2C receptor (Murray et al., 2010) and incomplete spinal cord injury leaves spared serotonergic fibers in the sensitized spinal cord (D'Amico et al., 2013) which both can cause spasticity by enhancing persistent inward currents.
evidence: Supported by citation to Murray et al., 2010

claim: Incomplete spinal cord injury leaves spared serotonergic fibers in the sensitized spinal cord which can cause spasticity by enhancing persistent inward currents.
source: Complete transection causes an up-regulation of the constitutively active 5HT2C receptor (Murray et al., 2010) and incomplete spinal cord injury leaves spared serotonergic fibers in the sensitized spinal cord (D'Amico et al., 2013) which both can cause spasticity by enhancing persistent inward currents.
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Amico et al., 2013

claim: KCC2, when located to the membrane, expels chloride- and potassium+ ions to regulate the reversal potential of GABAA responses.
source: KCC2, when located to the membrane, expels chloride- and potassium+ ions to regulate the reversal potential of GABAA responses; if membrane KCC2 is reduced, motor neurons become hyper-excitable (Boulenguez et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boulenguez et al., 2010

claim: If membrane KCC2 is reduced, motor neurons become hyper-excitable.
source: KCC2, when located to the membrane, expels chloride- and potassium+ ions to regulate the reversal potential of GABAA responses; if membrane KCC2 is reduced, motor neurons become hyper-excitable (Boulenguez et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boulenguez et al., 2010

claim: Complete transection of corticospinal pathways in the pyramids impairs locomotion and leads to increased spasms and excessive mono- and polysynaptic low threshold spinal reflexes in rats.
source: Here, we establish that complete transection of corticospinal pathways in the pyramids impairs locomotion and leads to increased spasms and excessive mono- and polysynaptic low threshold spinal reflexes in rats.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Treatment of affected forelimb muscles with an adeno-associated viral vector encoding human Neurotrophin-3 at a clinically-feasible time-point after injury reduced spasticity.
source: Treatment of affected forelimb muscles with an adeno-associated viral vector (AAV) encoding human Neurotrophin-3 at a clinically-feasible time-point after injury reduced spasticity.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Neurotrophin-3 normalized the short latency Hoffmann reflex to a treated hand muscle.
source: Neurotrophin-3 normalized the short latency Hoffmann reflex to a treated hand muscle as well as low threshold polysynaptic spinal reflexes involving afferents from other treated muscles.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Neurotrophin-3 normalized low threshold polysynaptic spinal reflexes involving afferents from treated muscles.
source: Neurotrophin-3 normalized the short latency Hoffmann reflex to a treated hand muscle as well as low threshold polysynaptic spinal reflexes involving afferents from other treated muscles.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Neurotrophin-3 enhanced locomotor recovery after bilateral pyramidotomy.
source: Neurotrophin-3 also enhanced locomotor recovery.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The balance of inhibitory and excitatory boutons in the spinal cord was normalized by Neurotrophin-3 treatment.
source: Furthermore, the balance of inhibitory and excitatory boutons in the spinal cord and the level of an ion co-transporter in motor neuron membranes required for normal reflexes were normalized.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The level of an ion co-transporter (KCC2) in motor neuron membranes required for normal reflexes was normalized by Neurotrophin-3 treatment.
source: Furthermore, the balance of inhibitory and excitatory boutons in the spinal cord and the level of an ion co-transporter in motor neuron membranes required for normal reflexes were normalized.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript
